set.body:
IDENTIFIED BY A HANDS-ON REVIEWER AS THE SINGLE MOST LIKELY POINT AT WHICH A TYPICAL USER ABANDONS
THE PACKAGE. Worth separating from the general error-message bead (bd-01KZY9B80RMYJD4QDAFS5ZBQSM)
because the cause is a field habit, not message style.

The error, verbatim:

  Error: Requested effects are not estimable: face, house, object, body.

Trigger: 4 condition dummies plus an intercept. Rank deficient, so the individual condition effects
genuinely are not estimable. THE PACKAGE IS CORRECT TO REFUSE and the reviewer said so - they
understood it in seconds and fixed it by dropping the intercept.

THE PROBLEM IS WHO ELSE WILL HIT IT. 'K condition regressors plus an intercept' is the standard
first-order design in SPM and FSL. Those tools accept it without complaint because they use a
pseudoinverse, and the user never notices because they only ever look at estimable CONTRASTS. So
the design that triggers this error is not a mistake a careless user makes - it is the design the
field's dominant software has trained everyone to write. Effectagram is the first tool in their
workflow that refuses it.

The message names WHAT failed and not WHY. It does not mention rank, does not identify which column
is collinear with which, and does not say that dropping the intercept resolves it. A user who has
never had to think about estimability - which is most of the target audience, because SPM never made
them - has no path from this message to a fix.

FIX, entirely within the existing house style. The package already writes messages of exactly this
shape at R/views.R:263 ('The RSA design is rank deficient; remove redundant RDMs.'):

  before  Requested effects are not estimable: face, house, object, body.

  after   Requested effects are not estimable: face, house, object, body.
          The design is rank deficient: the four condition columns sum to the intercept column.
          Either drop the intercept, or request estimable contrasts (e.g. face - house) instead
          of individual condition effects.

Note the second clause matters as much as the first. 'Drop the intercept' is the mechanical fix;
'request contrasts instead' is the statistically better answer and is what an SPM user actually
wants, since differences are what they were going to look at anyway.

CONTEXT FROM THE SAME TRIAL, which is why this ranks high. The reviewer - fluent in RSA, crossnobis,
R and GLMs - completed all three tasks in about 25 minutes of work on top of 20 minutes of reading,
without ever reading package source. Their estimate for others:

  RSA-literate R user                          half a day, mostly building the vocabulary map
  typical cognitive neuroscientist (SPM/FSL
  GUI plus moderate R)                         days, or gives up

and the two places they predicted the second group stalls are (a) constructing design and effects
matrices by hand with no multi-condition worked example, and (b) THIS ERROR, with no guidance. Both
are cheap to fix and both sit directly on the path from install to first result.
set.title: The estimability error is the most likely give-up point: SPM/FSL users are habituated to the design that triggers it
